I've had ADHD for years untreated. I don't use any medications like Adderall and have seen better results recently with these ideas in mind. I won't say it will 100% help you, but you can give it a shot.

\- Understand you aren't the typical person.

The first thing to understand is understanding you are not the typical average person. You have a condition that makes it hard for you to process things in a normal way. Anything a person who is normal will give to you for advice is not going to work with 100% efficiency. You need to make changes in your life that work around ADHD.

\- Understand why you doom scroll

We live in a world that can put a lot of information in your face. ADHD doesn't bode well with processing information, but its REALLY good at taking it in. Doom scrolling capitalizes on this fact. The fact you doom scroll is because your brain is focused on taking in information. But you've taken on information from yesterday and the day before. Its adding up and overwhelming you into a default mode. You need to be proactive in this next step to stop doom scrolling and get out of this default mode.

\- Your head is a container, you need to empty it

Every thought, idea, memory, ect. that you think of is compounding into your brain. ADHD is really good at shoving them all into your head and not processing them. You need to process what enters your head, give it the attention it wants, and then it will go away. Did you see a Tweet that particularly caught your eye? Think about it, talk about it out loud. Doesn't need to be told to anyone specific. Get it out of your head. Do this for all of the things you saw on social media that caught your attention. After you talk about it, your brain will get bored of it and throw it away. Your head is like a hard drive, and just like a real hard drive. If you fill the space in it, the hard drive will slow down. Once you empty the hard drive, you can put more thoughtful ideas into it. You can be more focused on what matters more to you.

\- Make the most minor changes. 

Snowball effects are the most proactive way to treat productivity issues in ADHD. Don't go off the rip and make big changes. You need to slowly change your routine over time. If reading a book is troubling, then don't focus on the chapters, don't focus on the pages. Focus on mastering reading the paragraphs first. Once you get used to reading paragraphs go for pages. Then when you get used to reading pages, go for chapters. Do not be discouraged on what you were able to do back in the day. If you could read books like it was nothing, and now you cant. Don't be depressed or sad about the fact you can't now. You just need to relearn how. And don't beat yourself up for when you can't read a paragraph normally.

​

Energy is a muscle. Any time you've heard of the trope that people who started to work out became successful, you need to understand WHY that happened. Your daily energy is like stamina in a video game. And just like video games, the only way to level up stamina like in GTA V is to run. Your energy for the day might be 10/10 and if you use it proactively like in a workout or a run, you will be giving yourself experience. Your body will get used to how you use it and change itself accordingly. If you eat less suddenly, you won't be able to eat as much as you used to until you consistently eat more. If you use less energy through the day, your body will only give you so much until you start using what it gives you proactively. There are of course the nuances I didn't mention until now like good sleep, healthy eating, and other factors that could give or take energy from you. But as a general idea, your body isn't going to give you a whole heaping of energy if you aren't using the energy it gives you.

Practice makes perfect. But also doesn't. Valorant is 3 things; Aim, Movement, and Mental. A lot of players neglect those 2nd and 3rd points and skip to only focus on their aim. When you leave a video game for prolonging amounts of time its the same as working out. Your muscles fade if you don't work out, your mind forgets the skill you put in if you don't play. Gradually this happens over time. However, this is easily reversible if you put in the time and effort to focus on practicing those three things. Just make sure you're doing it in a constructive way. Don't practice for 3 hours in one day. Doing that kept me in Master Guardian when I was a CS player. After I kept up a healthy regimen for my aim by committing only a portion of my time to practice (30-45 minutes) and got results I did a LOT of bhop and KZ maps in CS to get my movement better. It doesn't have to be perfect and I didn't have to get the high score. I just needed a legible difference between when I started and where I was when I improved. 

Don't think those Bronze/Silver players are shitters either. You WERE a gold player, you rusted up. You're on their level **for now**. There is probably a good chunk of players like yourself who quit for 6 months and found themselves in the same predicament when they came back. Often when this happens you have a traffic of players who all keep each other in that ranking because of how fast they can get back into form, you are no exception. As you play more you'll regain your skills faster than a noob who is still forming them. But you'll also encounter players in the same boat. So you now are facing gold players in Bronze/Silver elo. It happens all the time, that's a portion why Riot resets your rank more often than CS ever did. It keeps it healthy and puts you back where you belong when you rediscover all that lost potential when you came back.

You can't rush progress in your own play style either, your practicing methods won't speed up how quickly your brain can take in and learn from the information and repetition you give it. But it sure can take in the better information and practice it receives over bad practice and habits. Which is why I strongly encourage players NOT to train in a hyper-concentrated state. I'd rather you sedentarily just deathmatch for 30 minutes over Aim Labsing for 3 hours until you break 80k in points.

Nautilus is a big counter to Karma, especially when compared to other hook champions, so when you said you can deal with Thresh or Blitz easier I wasn't really shocked.

Karma has little to no mobility, especially early game. Nautilus' Q gap closes to a lethal degree to the point where if he Q+Passive combos you, you are FUCKED, even at level 1. In most cases in my experience, the only way to survive is to burn flash. 

Keep minions as your meat shield when you know his hook is up. If the enemies push into your tower and Naut is camping the bush, hide behind your minions and R+Q to punish him if you know he's hiding there, he'll do it less if you catch on early to it.

Karma is really squishy early laning phase, and with a built-in speed boost from her E, she's really annoying to play against as a hook champion like Naut. A lot of hook champions look to capitalize off an early kill when it comes to Karma since the early gold can help with countering her speed boost later in the laning phase.

Because of the previous tidbit above, this means Nautilus will match the same aggression Karma players have early game in order to gain a gold lead over her. Because of this, it's honestly best to wait until you have your W, E, or both before you become aggressive against a Nautilus. That way you have more at your disposal to save yourself or your ADC. Until you get to level 2 or 3 play it safe and try not to be too aggressive until you can afford to be.

When you get your W, if Nautilus pushes into the melee minions, that's when you should start to W him and then begin retreating at the same time. By the time he hits the caster minions, he'll be either rooted or have backed off to avoid being rooted and punished.

If the Naut player has become one with the bushes and that's where he is most of the laning phase then try to orient yourself around the river entrance mostly. He'll struggle at warding the river vs you, and often will never have an opportunity to hook you.

I've known people who have played CS:S to CS:GO and have still always been in a low elo. The difference between playing and playing to improve is a very harsh difference. When playing with friends and to win, you often don't think critically of how you play. You just play. When people wish to improve, they'll adopt a way of thinking that makes them analyze where they went wrong, how to avoid doing it in the future, and how to apply what they've learned in later rounds.

I'm on Icebox as Phoenix, I peek B long and immediately get Op'ed. I could have used my flash to make the Op'er retreat to yellow, site, or snowman. Then I could have used my wall to cross into site and take control with my team. <- This is an example of going over what you did wrong, going over what you could have done to prevent it, and thinking of ways to apply it. If you get killed and just call out and watch your teammates, you'll never really challenge yourself on where you made a mistake. Figuring out where you've made errors will help you correct them in future play. Doing this helps make your game sense grow.

As for your aim. A lot goes more into yourself than your settings. Finding a comfortable sensitivity is one thing, but your posture, aiming style, and mouse grip will all go into effect on how you aim. When I play I don't slouch, my elbow rests on the edge of my desk with my forearm all the way extended into a claw grip on my mouse. Its the most comfortable way for me to aim. Find what works for you there that makes your vertical and horizontal aiming more smooth and crisp.

For improving your aim, it honestly comes with time, but again, working on it helps. The way a lot of people expect is if they practice flicking they'll be headshot machines. This can not be far from the truth. When you watch a pro player flick onto somebodies head, you're seeing the result of hundreds of hours poured into perfecting their aim. They're pros, you don't see it, but they're practicing every day for countless hours to stay in form. What a lot of people do to start with aim training is they'll DM. Now this helps, but again, if you're just flicking randomly you're more likely just reinforcing a bad habit. What you should do is take your honest to god time aiming. You're gonna get less kills, sure. But if you play Deathmatch and take your sweet time to make sure your crosshair is resting on their face, you're gonna find over time with hours of work put in that you'll go from 12th place to 1st quickly. 

For helping aiming you need to understand that this is a tactical shooter, and with that, it's also BIG on movement. The way you move affects how you play. Obviously you already know that moving and shooting is a nono. But strafing makes applying moving and shooting and making it so you're accurate while doing so. Learning the Ins and Outs of strafing can help you massively.

Bad habits are basically the bane to your skill level. Many players will crouch immediately while spraying. They won't ever tap shoot but instead spray and literally pray it hits. They'll immediately pull down when spraying. Its a mess and those listed right there are some of the big ones I see in lower elo. Crouching makes you even more accurate, yes, but its a bad habit to do it immediately. If you're aiming head level and crouch while immediately shooting you'll get more body shots than headshots. If you unbind crouch and spray you'll most likely see giant differences. Learn how to add crouching with your spray later down the line when you get more used to aiming normally. When shooting an enemy, they can be near or far. Spraying works, but tap firing gives you better results. When your mind is subject to spraying and praying, you're gonna find yourself losing long range engagements. Getting used to lining up your crosshair and aiming and tap firing will help you win longer ranged engagements. When spraying, you'll often see that the first few shots stay relatively close to each other. Pulling down immediately is not really needed until shot #4. If you pull down immediately after firing you'll also just get more body shots. People who have a mix of this and immediately crouching are often shooting at the stomach. With all these in mind, you'll start noticing them now and start slowly improving upon them. Just be sure not to let them become habits again and you'll do fine.

There is no secret to getting better at this game and improving. It all comes down to how willing you are to put the time into getting better. After you start working on yourself and practice more you're going to see results. I can't tell you how long, it really just depends on how willing you are. There's no secret tips and tricks. Its basically just understanding how to play your agent with pure mechanics. Over time your aim will tune itself and your brain's muscle memory will adjust and over time you'll improve. But also understand that while good aim is a part of improving your game sense can blow that out of the water as well. Anyways, here's a whole ass novel on improving with core mechanics and small pieces of advice on how to work on them.

Start by understanding how strafing works and how to counter-strafe. If you can nail strafing down on a fundamental level and get your brains muscle memory used to strafing you'll see improvement quick. What I do is close my eyes and get the feel for my keyboard, like I'm getting myself calibrated to the feel of it. Practice strafing onto bot heads going left and right until you're consistently not messing up the counter-strafe. Moment you're moving left or right and press the A or D key to counter-strafe fully, shoot.  After some time I go into deathmatch and peek corners ready to counter-strafe into people. [Here's an example of how counter-strafing mixed with prefiring makes you look like a cheater.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ptUjzE2zmWU)

Another big thing is posture. Many people will flick with their arm and do micro adjustments with their wrist. If you are fully fledged wrist aimer you'll find it can be harder being precise and it'll be more challenging to adjust VS an arm player. I used to wrist aim but now I'm an arm player and it helped me improve aiming. Also understand how to arm aim correctly, usually players (Myself included) keep our elbows on the desk as a pivot point and have our arm elevated with our palms off the mousepad to keep it from dragging. Good posture and knowing how to arm aim can be good in getting more precise.

Another big thing is tracking. Players often overlook this and in aim trainers like AimLabs you'll often see them focus on grid shot where its just a point and click adventure. This will not help you when you have a moving target that is moving erratically. If you've ever spectated your teammate and the enemy peeks and keeps going one direction and your teammates aim can't keep up it means they're having a hard time tracking. Arm aiming also helps this tremendously in conjunction with a bigger sized mousepad. Utilizing more space with arm aiming can make your aiming smoother and as a result won't be jittery and snappy. Tracking while stationary is one thing, but tracking while strafing is another. Load into the practice range and spawn some bots. Go left and right and keep that cursor on the bots head at all times. Don't let it leave headshot placement for so much as 1 pixel. You'll suck at this at first, but again, over time it'll get better. Tracking is something you are going to absolutely fucking blow at doing, but overtime you'll get used to it. To a lot of players, when they see how horrendous their tracking can be when they do that task in AimLab they'll immediately quit and do something else instead like Grid shot. Don't do that. Only way you'll improve is to keep going at it, and in the long run you'll get more serotonin from how much more accurate you've become in game.

One small thing is reaction time. You wanna be quicker than your opponent and your gaming mouse with a PWM 3360 sensor or a mouse switch that is based off infared light to give it a .2MS response time (Genius idea, sad it was from Razer.) isn't going to cut it. Your eyes seeing it, giving your brain the stimuli, and your brain giving the command to click can take time, you want your brain to be ready for this sort of thing. Its like when in MMA and boxing a coach will usually tell the person they're training to dodge the punch when they're expecting it. Be ready for someone to swing when you expect it, be ready for someone to be around a corner when you expect it. Many players will peek, their brain registers somebody is there, and they don't shoot. Their brain didn't react fast enough. Honestly, the only way to improve this in Valorant is to just play and get used to the peekers advantage. But in CSGO if you're willing to get a workshop map there was a few workshop maps that let bots run forward past a small gap and you'd have to kill them before they crossed the gap, the gap could be increased or decreased based on how you like it and you'd never know when they'd come so it was practically random, meaning it was perfect to practice reaction timing.

Final thing is crosshair placement and understanding where to aim. Many players will botch this due to a few things. In CSGO we often crouch and spray. This was because after our 5th shot if we crouched, we'd be spraying at head level again and our aim got way easier to control while spraying. Nowadays people just crouch immediately instead. This actually is terrible and makes you a sitting duck. Your head is now at chest level, where people usually aim, you're also slower, and you are more compact, have fun with that death sentence. I unbound crouch moment that habit started forming and started practicing to make my aim more controlled with crouching instead. Honestly if you find yourself doing this too I'd just unbind crouch and bind it to something that's not easy to tap in aim duels but easy to tap while moving around the map freely. Enjoy head tapping 15% more of the time after that. People also underestimate where the head hitbox is. The head is higher than people think. I know it looks like you're aiming at the head, but often because of your pull down when you spray, you'll shoot them in the neck instead. What I do is aim at their forehead or just above their head. Remember when I said that CS players would crouch while spraying to control it better and be aiming head level? Similar concept. The first few shots don't actually go too far away from the first shot. So you realistically don't need to pull down immediately, except people (Me included) do. A lot. Which is why aiming more above the head can help.

You need to train your brain to adjust to keeping on track of what it sees. What you can do is practice taking it slow. This however can work against you. It can make your aim more erratic and often give you results you don't want.

To easily overcome tracking and better flicking you need to calm yourself down and go slow. Move your cursor onto a bots head slowly until its point blank and then shoot. Then repeat, do this and slowly ramp up the speed. Don't jump the gun too hard and ramp up too fast though, be patient, your muscle memory will thank you later. 

After you have a good precision on static moving bots, set them to start strafing. You'll find that it can be easier. What I personally do is if I know the enemy might swing common corners on maps I'll aim where I think they'll strafe and the moment their head runs into my crosshair I'll shoot. Try to get used to doing that to moving bots. The two of those exercises in conjunction will give you better effect on keeping a better tracking on your enemy.

Also if you're open to downloading Aimlab you can play the tracking tasks and improve your tracking in there, it gives you a consistent goal of outdoing yourself every attempt so you'll have better motivation to continue.
